title: T cells and B cells
objective: Distinguish T and B cell roles and explain clonal selection and memory.

steps.title: Two lymphocyte lineages
steps.body:
Adaptive immunity runs on **[[lymphocyte|lymphocytes]]**:

- **[[B cell|B cells]]** make **[[antibody|antibodies]]**: secreted proteins that bind a specific target.
- **[[T cell|T cells]]** come in types: **helper T cells** coordinate other cells; **cytotoxic T cells** kill infected cells.

Each lymphocyte carries one receptor with one specificity.

steps.title: Clonal selection and memory
steps.body:
You carry a huge repertoire of lymphocytes, each with a different receptor, made by shuffling gene segments. When one happens to match an invader, it is selected and **multiplies** (clonal expansion).

Some offspring become **[[memory cell|memory cells]]** that persist, which is why the second exposure is faster and stronger, and how vaccines work.

visual.alt: A row of lymphocytes with differently shaped receptors; an antigen matches one, which is selected and multiplies into many effector clones plus a long-lived memory cell.
visual.caption: The matching cell is selected and expands into clones plus memory.

steps.prompt: Match each cell to its job.
steps.explanation: Specificity plus memory is what the adaptive arm adds on top of innate defenses (B1).

steps.prompt: Why is the adaptive response slow the first time but fast the second?
options: The body forgets the pathogen entirely between the two exposures
First time, rare matching clones must be found and grown; later, memory waits
Because antibodies made the first time decay away almost instantly
Because the innate system actively blocks the first adaptive response
steps.explanation: Finding and expanding the right clone takes days. Pre-existing memory cells skip most of that on re-exposure, the basis of immunological memory and vaccination.

variants.setup: The same antigen is met twice, a few weeks apart.
variants.prompt: Why is the second response faster than the first?
options: The body forgets the pathogen entirely between the two exposures
First time, rare matching clones must be found and grown; later, memory waits
Because antibodies made the first time decay away almost instantly
Because the innate system actively blocks the first adaptive response
variants.reveal: Finding and expanding the right clone takes days the first time; pre-existing memory skips most of that on re-exposure.

steps.setup: A mouse is exposed to a new antigen, then re-exposed weeks later.
steps.prompt: How does the antibody response to the second exposure compare to the first?
steps.reveal: Memory B cells make the recall response faster and larger. That difference is the signature of adaptive memory.

variants.prompt: Compared with the first exposure, the antibody response to a second exposure of the same antigen is…
variants.explanation: Memory B cells make the recall response faster and larger — the signature of adaptive memory and the basis of vaccination.
